subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Peer Review: Science Checking Its Own Homework
description: A quick, practical guide to Peer Review: Science Checking Its Own Homework.

hook.text: A scientist claims a breakthrough. Before the world hears about it, other scientists tear it apart. That's peer review.

buildup.text: Peer review: independent experts evaluate a study's methods, data, and conclusions before publication.

discovery.text: It catches errors, biases, and overclaiming. Most submitted papers are rejected or require major revisions.

twist.text: Peer review is imperfect — reviewers have biases, prestigious authors get easier passes, and fraud can slip through.

climax.text: But it's the best system we have. Science without peer review is just someone's opinion with a lab coat.

punchline.text: Trust peer-reviewed science. But know the review system isn't perfect.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of peer review?
options: To have independent experts check methods, data, and conclusions
To decide who wins Nobel Prizes

details.summary: Peer review submits research to evaluation by qualified experts before publication. It is science's primary quality control mechanism, catching errors and flawed reasoning that the original researchers missed.
details.whyItMatters: Peer review is imperfect but indispensable. Understanding its strengths and limits helps you evaluate whether published research is trustworthy.
takeaways: Peer reviewers are independent experts who evaluate methods and conclusions
Peer review catches errors but cannot detect every form of fraud
Preprints bypass peer review and require extra scrutiny

faq.question: What are the main limitations of the peer review process?
faq.answer: Reviewers may lack expertise in specific sub-fields, have their own biases, or miss errors under time pressure. Peer review also struggles to catch outright fraud because it assumes good faith. It is a filter, not a guarantee.

faq.question: Should you trust a preprint the same way you trust a peer-reviewed paper?
faq.answer: No. Preprints have not undergone independent quality review. They are useful for rapid communication but require extra scrutiny of methods, data, and conclusions. During COVID-19, unvetted preprints were widely misinterpreted.
